strengths: L4Q addresses a practical NLP problem: adapting LLMs while producing weights that support efficient quantized inference. Merging LoRA updates before quantization provides a coherent way to eliminate the separate adapter inference path.
The memory results support the central engineering contribution. For 7B models, Table 1 reports 25.4 GB for L4Q versus 79.5 GB for QAT and 41.9 GB for QAT-LoRA, approaching LoRA’s 25.1 GB.

Evaluation spans seven model configurations, 3-bit and 4-bit quantization, and commonsense reasoning and MMLU benchmarks. Improvements recur across configurations, with some substantial gains at 3 bits, supporting usefulness beyond a single favorable example.

The paper includes actual inference measurements with quantized kernels, initialization and hyperparameter ablations, and detailed benchmark breakdowns. Together, these support a useful engineering contribution suitable for Findings.
weaknesses: The baseline comparisons support narrower conclusions than the broad superiority claims. QLoRA and LoftQ are modified to use uniform quantization, and learning rates differ substantially without a documented selection protocol. LoftQ’s frequent near-chance 3-bit performance warrants investigation before attributing the differences primarily to joint optimization.

Some efficiency comparisons are not controlled adequately. Appendix D uses sequence length 128 specifically for 33B L4Q, versus 2048 for other configurations, confounding its memory and training-time comparisons. The training-memory tradeoff also deserves prominence: Table 10 reports 25.4 GB for L4Q versus 7.9 GB for QLoRA at 7B.

Reproducibility details remain incomplete despite the extensive appendices. The manuscript does not provide its custom implementation, gradient-accumulation and checkpointing settings, LoRA scaling, or precise evaluation configurations. Equations 29–30 also need clearer notation: the elementwise clipping mask should act on the weight gradient before multiplication by the LoRA matrices.

No training-seed variability or confidence intervals are reported, although several leading margins are only 0.1–0.3 percentage points. Superiority is also not universal: on 3-bit LLaMA-2 13B MMLU 5-shot, L4Q scores 50.0 versus QLoRA’s 50.6. Claims of consistent superiority should be qualified.

The experiments do not fully isolate the proposed explanation for the gains. Matched-initialization ablations with frozen versus learned quantization parameters would distinguish joint optimization from initialization effects. Evaluation on one instruction-tuning corpus and multiple-choice benchmarks also limits conclusions about downstream adaptation and instruction-following quality.
